classification.difficultyReason: Compare corresponding angles, lengths and areas of a triangle and its translated image.

questions.mappingNote: The shared task investigates properties of a translation; measurement and triangle area support that investigation. Describe transformations is the closest primary catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–4 define translations, identify corresponding primed vertices, and state preservation of lengths and angles. Direct original prior-method references now supplied: Chapter6 PDF11 gives the protractor measurement steps; Chapter9 PDF22 gives triangle area as one half base times perpendicular height. Same-chapter pages2–4 supply correspondence and preservation of lengths/angles. Ruler length comparison remains the explicit original question instruction, not an unprovided algorithm assertion.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare corresponding angles, lengths and areas of a triangle and its translated image.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify a translation on a grid and apply its effects to points and corresponding intervals.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 extends the supplied grid-translation examples to an additional point and corresponding intervals. Parallelism is checked directly from equal grid directions.
questions.methodNote: Count horizontal and vertical grid movements between corresponding vertices; translate each point by the same movement and label its image with a prime. Translation preserves lengths and angles, and a non-identity translation has no fixed points.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify a translation on a grid and apply its effects to points and corresponding intervals.

classification.difficultyReason: Rotate relative to the specified centre and reconstruct each figure; the hardest cases require tracking a circle centre and its off-grid marked point separately, or determining the correct side of a rotated semicircular arc.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 directly applies Example 5 to square-grid figures. Parts a–b rotate points; c–d segments; e–f semicircular arcs; g–j polygon vertices; k–l circles and their marked points. The closest catalogue skill is transformations-coordinates, although the source grids have no printed axes.
questions.methodNote: A rotation preserves distance from its fixed centre. Example 5 rotates endpoints through right angles using a set square and ruler, then joins their images; the same construction applies to vertices, circle centres and marked points. Half-turn images lie opposite their originals through O.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct images of points, segments and curved figures under rotations about marked centres.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly taught fixed-point property of a nonidentity rotation to identify O as the only point that remains in place.

questions.mappingNote: Describing the fixed point of a rotation directly assesses the properties of transformations.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 states that a nonidentity rotation has exactly one fixed point, its centre. Pages 7–8 demonstrate rotating endpoints or vertices while keeping their distances from the centre unchanged.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the fixed point common to the nonidentity rotations in the preceding question.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct the rotated house including its doorway, then interpret preserved parallelism and compare the rectangular body's areas using grid dimensions; the named vertices scaffold which region to measure.

questions.mappingNote: The principal task is a graphical rotation and its preserved relationships. Rectangle area is additionally assessed in part c; ABCE deliberately excludes roof vertex D.
questions.methodNote: Use the stated rotation centre, angle and direction. Rotate the vertices while preserving distance from O, then join their images, following Examples 3–5. Apply the same rotation to the doorway and ceiling. For part c, count the rectangle's dimensions and multiply length by width.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a quarter-turn image about an external centre, compare parallel sides and calculate the preserved rectangular area.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply equal perpendicular distances across horizontal, vertical and diagonal axes, recognising fixed points and preserving connections; the hardest cases distinguish an unchanged circle from its reflected radius and reflect arrow directions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b and k assess vertical-axis reflection; d and e assess horizontal-axis reflection; g, h, l and m extend the same construction to diagonal axes and connected figures. Parts c, f and i assess separate points and fixed points; j assesses a circle and marked radius; n assesses direction under reflection; o assesses a concave region. Transform points on the Cartesian plane is the closest supplied catalogue skill, although these source grids have no numbered coordinates.
questions.methodNote: Draw a perpendicular from each point to the axis, mark the image at the same distance on the opposite side, then join corresponding vertices. Points on the axis remain fixed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reflects points, segments and composite figures in vertical, horizontal and diagonal axes, including fixed points and directed segments.

classification.difficultyReason: Carry out two ordered reflections, using the first image as the second input; diagonal axes require perpendicular-distance tracking and recognising vertices that become fixed on the second axis.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts apply the vertex construction of Example 6 twice, using the first reflected triangle as the input to the second reflection.
questions.methodNote: Reflect vertices along perpendiculars to the axis at equal distances, then join their images. Points on the axis remain fixed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct two successive reflections, including reflections in parallel diagonal axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct successive translated images, then combine horizontal and vertical shifts, accounting for cancellation of opposite directions.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess composition and description of translations; describe-transformations is the closest supplied catalogue skill. No coordinate labels or algebraic transformation rules are introduced.
questions.methodNote: Translate each vertex by the given horizontal and vertical shifts, join image vertices, then translate the first image again. Compare original and final positions to describe one equivalent translation, following Example 7.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Draw successive translations and combine horizontal and vertical shifts, including cancelling opposite shifts.

classification.difficultyReason: Track vertices through two turns using the circular grid, preserve their radii, and combine directed angles even when the first image coincides with the original.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts require graphical vertex rotation and the single equivalent turn; describe-transformations is the closest supplied skill. No coordinate-transformation shortcut is used.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 rotates endpoints or vertices around a fixed centre, preserving distance, then joins the images. Example 8 on page 15 combines successive rotations about the same centre. Page 16 introduces the combined-transformation exercise.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct two successive rotations and describe their combined effect about the same centre.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct reflections in both orders, including across a diagonal line, then compare final positions to determine whether reversing the order changes the result.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses graphical reflection and comparison of transformation order, so describe-transformations is the closest catalogue skill. Coordinate data are used only to specify editable geometry, not as a substitute student method.
questions.methodNote: Pages 11–12 teach reflecting each vertex to the opposite side of the axis at the same perpendicular distance and joining the image vertices. Pages 14–16 teach applying transformations successively and checking whether reversing their order changes the final image. Pages 3 and 7 support the comparison with translations and rotations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct successive reflections in two orders and compare the resulting images for perpendicular and intersecting reflection lines.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer a suitable rotation or reflection from corresponding vertices, choose its centre or axis, then determine and verify the translation needed to complete the mapping.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 asks for descriptions rather than coordinate calculations. Parts a and d combine a quarter-turn with a translation; parts b and c combine reflection in an existing side line with translation.
questions.methodNote: Rotate or reflect corresponding vertices, then translate the intermediate image by counting grid units. Example 9 explicitly permits different valid pairs of successive transformations; Example 10 establishes that order matters.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify an ordered pair of transformations from corresponding labelled triangles.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the specified reflection and translation in order, using the intermediate vertices and equal perpendicular distances from the fixed reflection line.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 directly applies Example 10 with a six-unit translation and extends it to translations parallel to the reflection axis.
questions.methodNote: Transform the vertices and join their images. Reflections preserve perpendicular distance from the axis; translations move every vertex the stated number of squares. Example 10 explicitly constructs and labels both successive images.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct successive reflections and translations, keeping track of their order.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a reflection and a parallel translation in each stated order, keeping the reflection line fixed and using each intermediate image for the second step.

questions.mappingNote: This task assesses graphical combinations of reflection and translation on an unnumbered square grid. The closest catalogue skill is describe-transformations; coordinate algebra is unnecessary.
questions.methodNote: Reflect vertices using perpendicular equal distances from the axis, join image vertices, and apply successive transformations in the stated order with prime and double-prime labels. Example 10 supplies the directly relevant two-order construction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct two successive transformations in each order, retaining intermediate and final images.

classification.difficultyReason: Track triangle vertices through a quarter-turn and reflection in each specified order, preserving distances from the rotation centre and reflection line.

questions.mappingNote: This unnumbered-grid construction combines rotation and reflection of a triangle, so describe-transformations is the closest catalogue skill. Coordinate transformation rules are not required by the source.
questions.methodNote: Rotate vertices about the specified centre while preserving radius; reflect vertices at equal perpendicular distances across the reflection line; join image vertices. Example 10 uses primes and double primes to distinguish successive images and demonstrates that order matters.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct two successive transformations in each of two different orders.

classification.difficultyReason: Plot each coordinate point, apply the same supplied horizontal and vertical shift, and read and label its image coordinates.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed method is translating coordinates, supported by plotting and labelling original and image points. The supplied power-curve reuse candidate is a different task and is inapplicable.
questions.methodNote: Translations shift every point by the same horizontal and vertical amounts. Example 11a, b demonstrates coordinate translations; the earlier translation examples demonstrate counting grid units and labelling images with primes. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the same stated translation to four given points and plot their images.

classification.difficultyReason: Plot each original–image pair and interpret their horizontal and vertical displacement, including movement across zero and a purely vertical translation.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed response describes coordinate displacement under translation.
questions.methodNote: Plot the original point and its image, then count horizontal and vertical grid units from the original to the image. Pages 2–3 explain translation as a shift without turning; page 19 Example 11 connects translations to coordinates. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plot given point-image pairs and count horizontal and vertical displacement.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught anticlockwise quarter-turn about the origin, locate images in the appropriate quadrants, and recognise that the centre remains fixed.

questions.mappingNote: The assigned question uses the graphical quarter-turn method from Example 11c, d. Page 20 directs students to use graph paper, draw labelled axes and give image coordinates; one shared plane is permitted.
questions.methodNote: Rotate a point about the given centre through the stated angle and direction while preserving its distance from the centre. Example 11d demonstrates an anticlockwise quarter-turn on a labelled Cartesian plane. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply one quarter-turn anticlockwise about the origin to four points, including the fixed origin.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply one half-turn about the origin to four points, including the fixed origin.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed operation is a 180-degree rotation of coordinate points, matching transformations-coordinates.
questions.methodNote: Use a graphical rotation about the origin, retaining distance from the centre. Page 19 Example 11g illustrates a half-turn; page 6 states the fixed-centre and equal-distance properties. Page 20 permits a single labelled number plane for all parts. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply one half-turn about the origin to four points, including the fixed origin.

classification.difficultyReason: Reflect each plotted point across the x-axis at equal perpendicular distance, retaining points on the axis and reading the image coordinates.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 applies Example 11e to four coordinate points. Page 20 supplies the exercise-wide requirements for labelled axes, labelled points and image coordinates.
questions.methodNote: Reflect each point along a perpendicular to the axis, keeping its distance from the axis unchanged. Points on the axis stay fixed. Example 11e demonstrates reflection in the x-axis graphically. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plot four given points and reflect each in a coordinate axis, including a fixed point.

classification.difficultyReason: Reflect the given vertices across the y-axis, keep the vertex on the axis fixed, and join the already determined images to form the reflected triangle.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 directly applies vertex reflection in the y-axis to three given Cartesian points and then their triangle.
questions.methodNote: Reflect each vertex along a perpendicular to the axis, keeping equal distances on opposite sides; points on the axis remain fixed. Join the reflected vertices. Example 11f demonstrates reflection in the y-axis, and Example 6 demonstrates constructing the image triangle. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reflect three given vertices in the y-axis and join their images.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply two specified axis reflections in sequence, track intermediate and final coordinates, and recognise that a point on the first axis stays fixed.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 combines the two axis reflections from Example 11 in the successive-image format of Example 12. The directly assessed skill is transforming points on the Cartesian plane.
questions.methodNote: Pages 11–12 construct reflection images at equal perpendicular distances from the axis and identify points on the axis as fixed. Example 11 on page 19 applies reflections in coordinate axes. Example 12 on page 20 plots successive transformations with prime and double-prime labels; the exercise instructions require labelled number planes and image coordinates. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply two reflections in the specified order and plot the intermediate and final images.

classification.difficultyReason: Link reflection and downward translation in the stated order, applying the translation to the reflected coordinates while preserving each x-coordinate.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses successive coordinate transformations, so transformations-coordinates is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 11 demonstrates reflection in the x-axis and translations on a labelled Cartesian plane. Example 12 plots original, intermediate and final images for two successive transformations. Apply reflection first, then move the resulting image four units down. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply a reflection followed by a translation, retaining the correct transformation order.

classification.difficultyReason: Plot and join the given vertices, then obtain image coordinates by subtracting four from y and reflecting the resulting points in the y-axis.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the sequential graphical method of Example 12, replacing its clockwise rotation with the reflection in the y-axis requested here. Example 11f supplies the reflection model.
questions.methodNote: Example 11 illustrates translation and reflection using coordinate plots. Example 12 plots this same original triangle, translates it 4 units down and applies a second transformation to the intermediate image. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plot a triangle and apply two transformations in the specified order.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow a straightedge-and-compass construction, identify eight reflection axes and distinguish the symmetry of an inscribed square.

questions.mappingNote: The principal assessed reasoning is line and rotational symmetry of the constructed octagon and its inscribed square. The symmetry-of-graphs catalogue entry explicitly covers plane shapes.
questions.methodNote: Use the supplied three-stage square-and-circumcircle construction. Reflection axes map a figure onto itself; rotational order is 360° divided by the smallest matching rotation. Page 25 names the octagon and demonstrates equal central-angle polygon construction; page 26 applies symmetry to regular polygons. The original question supplies the complete square/circumcircle/octagon scaffold. Direct original Chapter13 PDF18 supplies right-angle construction; PDF19 supplies perpendicular bisectors and explicitly locating an interval midpoint. These are prior construction references, not a claim that a separate full square procedure is printed there.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Follow a straightedge-and-compass construction, identify eight reflection axes and distinguish the symmetry of an inscribed square.

classification.difficultyReason: Link the taught hexagon and midpoint constructions using explicit steps, interpret the numbered vertices as a clock face, and identify both families of dodecagon symmetry axes.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced assessed skill is identifying reflection and rotational symmetry of a regular polygon. The radius and complete construction steps are retained; question 4 is referenced as a method rather than as a source of missing givens.
questions.methodNote: Use question 4's radius-stepping hexagon construction, then the opposite-midpoint construction illustrated for the octagon on page 26. Apply the reflection-axis and smallest-rotation definitions on pages 22–23 and regular-polygon symmetry on page 26. Direct original Chapter13 PDF19 supplies the equilateral-triangle 60-degree construction and perpendicular-bisector/midpoint construction. The original question retains its full construction scaffold; same-chapter symmetry references remain.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Follow a multistage compass construction, interpret its vertices and identify both forms of symmetry.

classification.difficultyReason: Extend the taught regular-polygon rotation pattern to recognise that each vertex gives one matching position, so rotational order equals the number of sides without drawing.

questions.mappingNote: The task generalises the taught regular-polygon example to 36 and 37 sides. The closest catalogue skill directly assesses rotational symmetry of plane shapes.
questions.methodNote: Pages 22–23 define rotational order through repeated smallest rotations in a full turn. Page 25 relates equally spaced central rays to the number of sides; page 26 demonstrates that a regular pentagon has rotational order 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the relationship between the number of sides of a regular polygon and its rotational symmetry.

classification.difficultyReason: Count horizontal and vertical grid movements between corresponding points.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly apply the grid-counting method from Example 1; no coordinate calculation or later transformation method is required.
questions.methodNote: A translation shifts every point by the same horizontal and vertical distances without turning the figure. Example 1 describes movement by counting grid units between corresponding vertices.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count horizontal and vertical grid movements between corresponding points.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the specified 60-degree clockwise rotation into two grid divisions, preserve each endpoint's circle, and join the image endpoints.

questions.mappingNote: This task directly applies Example 3 with two clockwise divisions rather than four. The closest supplied skill is describing transformations of shapes; coordinate rules are not assessed.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 establishes fixed distance from the centre and 30-degree polar divisions. Page 7 Example 3 rotates interval endpoints by counting clockwise divisions on the same circles, then joins their images. Page 8 reinforces rotating endpoints and preserving distance.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rotate two endpoints through two marked radial divisions while preserving their distances from the centre.

classification.difficultyReason: Move each vertex two 45-degree divisions clockwise on its existing circle, then label and join the images using the taught circular-grid method.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 applies the same vertex-by-vertex circular-grid method, with clockwise direction explicitly supplied.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 define rotation and circular grids. Page 7 Example 4 rotates each triangle vertex through two 45-degree divisions, preserving its circle, and joins the images. Page 8 also demonstrates preserving distance from O during a clockwise quarter-turn.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply a specified quarter-turn to three vertices using the supplied circular grid.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a quarter-turn image of three vertices about a supplied centre.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly applies the taught graphical rotation method to a triangle through 90 degrees anticlockwise.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–8 establish centre, angle and direction; rotate vertices while preserving distance from O, then join their images. Page 8 demonstrates construction on a square grid.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a quarter-turn image of three vertices about a supplied centre.

classification.difficultyReason: Reflect each vertex across the supplied vertical axis by counting equal horizontal grid distances, then join the images.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly applies the taught graphical reflection method to a triangle across a vertical axis. No numerical coordinate labels are introduced.
questions.methodNote: Reflect each vertex along a perpendicular to the axis, preserving its distance from the axis, then join the image vertices; pages 11–12, Example 6.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reflect three vertices across a vertical axis using perpendicular grid distances.

classification.difficultyReason: Plot each coordinate pair, apply the specified rightward and upward movements, and read the image coordinates using the taught procedure.

questions.mappingNote: Each part requires plotting a given point, moving it 3 units right and 1 unit up, and reading its image coordinates. Transforming Cartesian points is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 describe translation as moving points a specified horizontal and vertical distance without turning. Page 19 Example 11 applies translations to a point on a Cartesian grid. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plot three given points and apply the same horizontal and vertical translation to each.

classification.difficultyReason: Plot corresponding points and interpret their horizontal and vertical displacement, including movement across the horizontal axis and a purely vertical translation.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed result is a translation description from given coordinate pairs; coordinates-translation-reflection is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 describe translations by horizontal and vertical movement and identify corresponding primed points. Page 19 Example 11 represents transformations using coordinates on a Cartesian grid. Plot each original point and its image, then count the horizontal and vertical grid displacement. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plot two given points and count their horizontal and vertical displacement.

classification.difficultyReason: Plot three points in different quadrants and find their images under a quarter-turn about the origin.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is finding coordinates after rotation about the origin.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 rotates vertices through the stated angle while preserving distance from the centre. Page 19 Example 11(d) applies a 90° anticlockwise rotation about the origin and shows (1,3) mapping to (−3,1) on a Cartesian plane. Use plotted quarter-turns and read image coordinates. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plot three points in different quadrants and find their images under a quarter-turn about the origin.

classification.difficultyReason: Plot each point and place its image at the same horizontal position and equal distance on the opposite side of the x-axis.

questions.mappingNote: Each part plots a given point and uses equal vertical distances from the x-axis to locate its image.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 constructs a reflected point at equal perpendicular distance on the opposite side of the reflection axis. Page 19 Example 11(e) applies reflection in the x-axis to a coordinate point. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plot three integer-coordinate points and reflect them in a coordinate axis.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the smallest turn preserving each whole figure and count repetitions in a full turn; the open curve requires recognising a half-turn about its central midpoint.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess rotational symmetry directly; the general plane-shape symmetry skill covers the petals and open curve as well as the quadrilaterals.
questions.methodNote: Find the smallest rotation that makes the figure fit exactly onto itself, then count repetitions in a full turn, as in the rotational-symmetry explanation and Example 13.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the number of matching positions during one full turn for four familiar figures.

classification.difficultyReason: Draw two successive translations and combine their horizontal and vertical movements.

questions.mappingNote: Apply this vertex-shifting method twice, then combine the horizontal movements and vertical movements separately.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 translates each vertex by counting horizontal and vertical grid units, joins the translated vertices and labels the image. Example 1 explains horizontal and vertical movements in either order.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Draw two successive translations and combine their horizontal and vertical movements.

classification.difficultyReason: Track vertices through two rotations on the supplied angular grid, then combine their directed angles, distinguishing addition from cancellation when directions differ.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses graphical rotations and their combined effect, so describe-transformations is the closest supplied skill. Coordinate transformation rules are unnecessary.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 Example 3 rotates endpoints by counting 30-degree divisions while retaining distance from O; Example 4 rotates triangle vertices and joins their images. Page 23 confirms angle and centre conventions for rotations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct successive rotations in opposite or matching directions and identify their equivalent rotation.

classification.difficultyReason: Plot points and track two successive reflections in the specified order.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task combines coordinate plotting with successive coordinate-axis reflections, so transformations-coordinates is the closest advanced assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 11–12 teach reflection by placing each image at equal perpendicular distance on the other side of the axis. Page 16 preserves the order of successive transformations. Page 19 Example 11 demonstrates reflections in the coordinate axes; page 20 Example 12 plots original, intermediate and final images on one plane. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plot points and track two successive reflections in the specified order.

classification.difficultyReason: Maintain each intermediate point through two specified translations and read the final coordinates, tracking opposing horizontal movements and reinforcing vertical movements.

questions.mappingNote: Each part uses the same two successive translations and graphical reading of coordinates.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 teaches shifting points by the stated horizontal and vertical distances. Page 19 Example 11 represents translated points on a coordinate plane. Page 20 Example 12 retains intermediate and final images for successive transformations. Direct original Chapter12 PDF6 Example5 gives four-quadrant coordinate plotting, signs, x/y coordinate directions and joined-vertex plotting in Example6. Same-chapter transformation methods remain as already referenced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply two successive translations, plot intermediate images and read final coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer a valid two-step mapping from corresponding vertices without supplied intermediate images, choosing a rotation or reflection and a compensating translation; the oblique reflection requires particular spatial analysis.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess describing successive shape transformations from grids, rather than calculating Cartesian coordinates. The closest skill is describe-transformations.
